newsitem.title: USA: Alcoholics' "match" to treatment falls short.
newsitem.headline: Alcoholics' "match" to treatment falls short.

text.p: An attempt to improve treatment of alcoholism by precisely matching a patient to the most appropriate treatment option has fallen short of expectations, researchers said on Tuesday.
That meant a setback for patient "matching," whereby a patient is given extensive screening and then assigned to a treatment programmes that appears best for that particular case.
But the study also showed that patients can get comparable results from any of the three common treatment approaches tested without any elaborate matching procedures.

"These findings challenge the notion that patient-treatment matching is necessary in alcoholism treatment," said Dr. Enoch Gordis, director fo the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA).

"These findings are good news for treatment providers and for patients who can have confidence that any one of these treatments, if well-delivered, represents the state-of-the-art in behavioural treatments" he added.
About 9 percent of U.S. adults can be considered alcoholic or having the less severe form known as alcohol abuse. Of those who get treatment, at least half will relapse in two to four years.
In recent years, the idea of matching people to treatment gained popularity. But the eight-year study confirmed only one of 11 possible matches.

More than 1,700 patients in the study were screened and evaluated for several traits, among them severity of their alcohol involvement, their gender, motivational readiness to change and the social support for drinking versus abstinence.

They were then matched with one of three behavioural therapies -- a 12-step programme similar but not identical to Alcoholics Anonymous; a cognitive-behavioural approach in which they worked on developing skills to avoid relapse; or a motivational enhancement therapy designed to help them build up their own motivational skills to stay sober.
In addition, the patients were divided into inpatient and outpatient groups.

In 10 of the 11 matches, the researchers after an eight-year study found that there were no statistical differences in how well the patients fared. Overall, all the participants showed significant and sustained improvement in how much they were able to remain abstinent, and how much they drank on days they lapsed. But there was little evidence that "matching" made a difference.
The researchers said that their findings did not rule out the benefits of matching in helping patients choose therapies for other mental or psychiatric problems.

But for problem drinking, "a logical next step for alchoholism treatment research is to test our quite excellent behavioural treatments in conjunction with promising pharmacological treatments for alcohol," said Dr. Richard Fuller, an NIAAA official who helped oversee Project Match.
